newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Mining companies need size, diversity.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Mining companies need size, diversity.

text.p: LONDON, June 30, Reuter) - The scale, cost and risk of present-day minerals projects mean that mining companies will tend to get bigger and to diversify their interests, the head of the mining and metals unit of syndicated loan leader Chase Securities Inc said.

James Griffin, who is Managing Director of Chase's Global Mining and Metals Group, said in an interview that the mining business was changing rapidly, encompassing new technology, more surface mining, longer project life and larger economies of scale.
"Mining companies are getting larger, as the projects are getting larger..and they are diversifying by having three legs to the stool," he said.

A typical company now would perhaps have a base metal project, precious metal development, as well as a coal holding, which guards against the cyclical nature of one element of the portfolio, he said.
The size of current mining projects means also more expense in development and more joint-ventures such as took place at Escondida and El Abra in Chile and Alumbrera in Argentina.

"You are moving towards porphyry projects of $2/3 billion with 50-year mine lives. It is a different game from 10/20 years ago, when a typical project might have been a 2/3 years highgrade underground with a return on capital of six months," Griffin said.
Technology changes, such as the well-established solvent extraction-electrowon (SX-EW) in copper and bio-leaching in gold are another facet in a changing business.
"It means a large percentage of the costs will go into infrastructure and it means a longer tenure of debt," he added.
Similarly, raising the finance is changing, as many projects are located in countries that were deemed to be politically risky.
As country risk is reduced capital for exploration and development can be raised from sources other than quasi-governmental and international finance agencies that are the first port of call.
"Once a country improves on its risk rating the next sources are the commercial banks," Griffin added.
And as the cycle improves further, then institutional and pension fund capital becomes available.
If during the same time the project has successfully been completed, then the sponsors enjoy both reduced technical risk as well as an improved host country risk environment, he said.
Chase is a major player in mining finance, topping the 1996 syndications league table by handling credit totalling $13.777 billion, some 40 percent of the market.
Among the metals, copper and gold are the favoured sectors for financing activity.

Copper prices are consistently holding above the $1.00/lb level, with money markets look at long-term prices in the $0.80/0.85 area to see whether or not there is sufficent cash/flow coverage for the debt.
"Many of the new projects have costs in the $0.50/0.55 range, so it is a very healthy industry," Griffin said.
In gold, the picture is somewhat different, in that the North American companies will buy to add to their reserves to justify high P/E (price/earnings) ratios.
"We will see more mergers and acquisitions and more consolidation as it becomes more cost affective to replace reserves with acquisitions then exploration," he said.
Meanwhile, despite the growth in company and project size, as well as the fall-out from the Bre-X affair, there is still a big role for the small junior companies.
"They can drill a hole less expensively. They can get into a country a little earlier than the majors. If there is a good prospect they can do a little trenching, and drill a couple of holes."

"Post Bre-x juniors will still be there, but it is going to be more difficult for them to get lines of credit and do steps towards reserve confirmation, finance feasability, and construction," Griffin said.
So the major companies who inevitably buy-in to a discovery, will benefit.
"They will have the opportunity to get there sooner which by definition is less expensive," he said.
